name: Liquidity Stress Testing
title: Liquidity Stress Testing
answer: Liquidity stress testing is the practice of modelling whether a firm can meet its cash and collateral obligations under adverse conditions, such as deposit runs, frozen wholesale funding markets or a ratings downgrade. In treasury work it sits alongside regulatory ratios like the liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio, but it goes further by asking what happens when assumptions break. The scope covers contractual cash flows, behavioural balances, contingent off balance sheet draws and the market value of liquid assets under stress. It applies to banks, insurers, fund managers and large corporates with material funding or collateral exposures.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Liquidity stress testing is the practice of modelling whether a firm can meet its cash and collateral obligations under adverse conditions, such as deposit runs, frozen wholesale funding markets or a ratings downgrade. In treasury work it sits alongside regulatory ratios like the liquidity coverage ratio and the net stable funding ratio, but it goes further by asking what happens when assumptions break. The scope covers contractual cash flows, behavioural balances, contingent off balance sheet draws and the market value of liquid assets under stress. It applies to banks, insurers, fund managers and large corporates with material funding or collateral exposures.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a cash flow engine that maps positions to maturity buckets and counterparties, fed by core banking, treasury management and market data systems. Firms typically hold a data warehouse or lake that consolidates ledger balances, trade records, collateral schedules and funding plans, with a scenario layer that applies shocks to those inputs. Reporting is usually delivered through a treasury dashboard or a regulatory reporting stack, and larger institutions run the calculation on grid or cloud compute because full balance sheet simulation across many scenarios is heavy. Spreadsheets still appear at smaller firms, but they struggle with version control and audit trail.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts define scenarios, ranging from idiosyncratic firm specific events to market wide shocks, then translate each into shocks on deposit outflow rates, wholesale funding rollover, asset haircuts and drawdowns on committed lines. The cash flow engine projects inflows and outflows over a horizon, often thirty days and ninety days, and computes the resulting funding gap or surviving liquidity buffer. Behavioural assumptions, such as how quickly retail deposits leave or how much of a committed facility is drawn, are the hardest part and are usually calibrated from historical episodes and expert judgement. Results are reviewed against limits and appetite statements, and the process is repeated on a schedule and after any material change in the balance sheet.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership normally sits with the treasurer or chief financial officer, with the board setting risk appetite and the asset liability committee reviewing results. Regulators in most major jurisdictions require documented scenarios, defined assumptions and evidence that the outputs feed into funding and contingency planning. Internal audit and validation teams test the models, and the assumptions behind them are expected to be challenged rather than accepted. Provenance matters because a stress result is only as good as the data and judgement behind it, so firms keep an audit trail linking each number to its source system and each assumption to its owner. This page describes practice and is not legal, regulatory or financial advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Supervisors continue to push for more frequent and more severe scenarios, and for stress results to be tied directly to contingency funding plans rather than filed and forgotten. Machine learning is being applied to behavioural assumptions, particularly deposit attrition and collateral haircuts, though explainability remains a hurdle for regulatory acceptance. Climate, cyber and intraday liquidity scenarios are moving from pilot work into regular reporting. The direction of travel is toward faster runs, more granular data and stress testing that informs day to day funding decisions rather than only periodic submissions.
